'''Choudhry Rahmat Ali'''{{efn|({{Langx|ur|{{nastaliq|چودھری رحمت علی}}}}; {{IPA|ur|tʃoː(ɦ)dəɾi ɾɛɦmət əli|lang}}}} (16 November 1897 – 3 February 1951) was a [[Muslim nationalism|Muslim nationalist]] activist who is credited with coining the name "Pakistan" for a separate Muslim homeland in [[British Raj|British India]] and is sometimes regarded as the originator of the [[Pakistan Movement]].

Born in [[Balachaur|Balachaur, Punjab]], Rahmat Ali got his education in [[Lahore]]. His seminal contribution was when he was a law student at the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1933, in the form of a pamphlet "[[s:Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?|''Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?'']]", also known as the "[[Pakistan Declaration]]".{{sfnp|Aziz|1987}}<ref name="Malik2003">
{{citation |last=Malik |first=Rashida |title=Iqbal: The Spiritual Father of Pakistan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KSluAAAAMAAJ&q=Gujjar |year=2003 |publisher=Sang-e-Meel Publications |isbn=978-969-35-1371-4}}
</ref><ref name="ʻ Choudhry Rehmat Ali 2009 ">
{{citation |last=ʻBilal |first=Safwan |title=Complete Works of
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F5QBAAAAMAAJ&q=Gujjar |year=1978 |publisher=National Commission on Historical and Cultural Research}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web
| title = Death anniversary of Ch Rehmat Ali being observed 4 February 1951
| date = 14 February 2008
| publisher = Dunya News
| url=https://dunyanews.tv/en/Pakistan/157528-Death-anniversary-of-Ch-Rehmat-Ali-being-observed}}
</ref> The pamphlet was addressed to the British and Indian delegates to the [[Third Round Table Conference]] in London.{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|pp=49–50}} The ideas did not find favour with the delegates or any of the politicians for close to a decade. They were dismissed as students' ideas particularly by [[Muhammad Ali Jinnah]] but, by 1940, the Muslim politicians in the subcontinent came around to accept them, leading to the [[Lahore Resolution]] of the [[All-India Muslim League]], which was immediately dubbed the "Pakistan Resolution" in the press.

After the creation of Pakistan, Ali returned from England in April 1948, planning to stay in the country, but his belongings were confiscated and he was expelled by Prime Minister [[Liaquat Ali Khan]]. In October 1948, Ali left empty-handed. He died on 3 February 1951 in Cambridge "destitute, forlorn and lonely".{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|pp=87–88}} The funeral expenses of insolvent Ali were covered by [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]] on the instructions of its Master - [[Edward Welbourne]]. Ali was buried on 20 February 1951 at [[Cambridge City Cemetery]].

==Early life==
Rahmat Ali was born on 16 November 1897 in the village of [[Balachaur]] in the Garhshankar Tahsil{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=1}} of [[Hoshiarpur District]] in the [[Punjab (British India)|Punjab Province]] of [[British Raj|British India]]. He was born into a [[Punjabi Muslims|Punjabi Muslim]] family. His father, Haji Shah Muhammad, had two wives; Rahmat Ali was the son of the second. She died when he was too young to remember her, and he was raised by his stepmother.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=1}} According to the historian [[Khursheed Kamal Aziz|K. K. Aziz]],<ref>{{harvp|Aziz|1987|p=28}}: "In the Gujjar caste his sub-caste or ''got'' was (Gorsi) ."</ref> who knew Ali personally, he was from the Gorsi clan of [[Gurjar|Gujjar]] tribe.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rahi |first=Javaid |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KI1pEAAAQBAJ&dq=choudhry+rahmat+ali+gujar&pg=PA621 |title=The Gujjars Vol: 01 and 02 Edited by Dr. Javaid Rahi (Page_621) |publisher=Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture, Languages, Jammu |year=2012 |pages=621 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=All but Forgotten: Choudhary Rahmat Ali, the Inventor and First Champion of Pakistan |url=https://thewire.in/history/choudhary-rahmat-ali-the-inventor-of-pakistan |access-date=17 May 2023 |website=The Wire |quote="When Now or Never was published, Ali was 36 years old. Born in a Gujjar Muslim family in Balachaur in the Hoshiarpur district of Punjab in 1897. Ali graduated from Islamia Madrassa, Lahore in 1918 and taught at Aitchison College, Lahore for a while before joining Punjab University to study law. It appears that after his legal studies he served as a legal adviser to a Baluchi landlord in which capacity he was able to save enough money and in 1930, move to England to join Emmanuel College, Cambridge. Subsequently, he obtained a BA degree in 1933 and MA in 1940 from the University of Cambridge. In 1943, he was called to the Bar, from Middle Temple, London.'}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
As Balachaur was a small village, Ali had to continue his education in the town of [[Rahon]] where there was a middle school.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=3}} After leaving middle school Ali travelled to [[Jalandhar]] in 1910 to enroll in the [[D.A.V. College Managing Committee|Saindas Anglo Sanskrit High School]] - then after matriculation in 1912, he then joined Islamia College Lahore later that year. He passed the intermediate examination in 1915 with English, history, maths and Persian as his subjects of study, he went on to earn a BA degree from Islamia college in 1918, reading English, economics and Persian. During his time at the college he had been secretary of the college debating union as well as being secretary and vice president of his tutorial group - additionally he was editor of the college magazine ''Crescent''.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=4}}

Outside of college, Ali served as assistant editor of Kashmir, a well-known paper of that time founded and edited by Munshi Muhammad Dın Fauq Kashmiri. Ali had written several articles on Indian history and politics, arguing that northern or north western India was the homeland of the Muslims and that they had the right to rule over it. One of these articles cost him his job, entitled "مغرب کی کورانا تقلید" i.e. "Maghrıb ky Korana Taqlid" (Blind Imitation of the West).{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=5}} The article soon attracted the notice of the British authorities, prompting the Deputy Commissioner of Lahore, Henry Phillips Tollinton,<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Supplement to The London Gazette, 4 June 1917
 |url=https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/30111/supplement/5461/data.pdf
 |website=The Gazette
 |publisher=His Majesty's Stationery Office
 |date=4 June 1917
 |access-date=14 December 2025
 |language=English
}}</ref> to summon Fauq to his office. There, Tollinton issued a stern reprimand and cautioned him of potential punitive measures should such an incident recur. In the aftermath of this confrontation, Fauq dismissed Ali from his position.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=6}}   
 
After graduating from [[Government Islamia College, Civil Lines, Lahore|Islamia College Lahore]] in 1918, he taught at [[Aitchison College|Aitchison College Lahore]] and after this, he served as the Chief Advisor to Sir Nawab Murad Buksh Khan Mazari for six years. During this period, he also took on the role of teacher to Mazari's children, including Mir [[Balakh Sher Mazari]] who would later become the [[Caretaker Prime Minister of Pakistan]], and Sardar [[Sherbaz Khan Mazari]], who was the [[Leader of the Opposition (Pakistan)]] and the head of the [[Movement for the Restoration of Democracy]], before joining [[University of the Punjab|Punjab University]] to study law. In 1930, he decided to move to England to study law at [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]] which he joined in 1931. Subsequently, he obtained a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA degree]] in 1933 and [[Master of Arts|MA]] in 1940 from the [[University of Cambridge]]. In 1933, he published a pamphlet, "[[s: Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?|Now or Never]]", coining the word ''Pakistan'' for the first time.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1189425|title=Smokers' Corner: The map man|last=Paracha|first=Nadeem F.|date=21 July 2015|website=Dawn|language=en|access-date=19 January 2019}}</ref> In 1943, he was called to the Bar, from [[Middle Temple]], London.<ref>{{Cite web |date=16 November 2022 |title=Chaudhry Rehmat Ali remembered on his 125th birth anniversary |url=https://www.nation.com.pk/16-Nov-2022/chaudhry-rehmat-ali-remebered-on-his-125th-birth-anniversary |access-date=17 May 2023 |website=The Nation |language=en-US |quote="Chaudhry Rehmat Ali was born in a Muslim Gujjar family in Hoshiarpur District of Indian Punjab on November 16, in 1897. He is credited with coming up with the name for a separate Muslim homeland in South Asia, PAKISTAN. After graduating from Islamia Madrassa, Lahore in 1918 he taught at Aitchison College before joining Punjab University (PU) to study law.'}}</ref>

In 1946, he founded the [[Pakistan National Movement]] in England. Until 1947, he continued publishing various booklets about his vision for South Asia. The final [[Partition of India]] disillusioned him due to the mass killings and mass migrations it ended up producing. He was also dissatisfied with the [[Radcliffe Line|distribution of areas]] between the two countries in The Greatest Betrayal he wrote of the six "deadly blows" that he believes Jinnah had dealt against the Muslims by accepting a smaller Pakistan than Ali had envisioned<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rahmat Ali
 |first=Choudhary
 |title=The Greatest Betrayal
 |publisher=Self-published pamphlet
 |location=Cambridge
 |year=1947
 |language=English
}}</ref> and considered it a major reason for the disturbances. {{Citation needed|date=January 2024}}

== Philosophy ==
Ali's writings, in addition to those of [[Muhammad Iqbal]] and others, were major catalysts for the formation of Pakistan. He offered the name "[[Eastern Bengal and Assam|Bangistan]]" for a Muslim homeland in the [[Bengal]] region, and "[[Hyderabad State|Osmanistan]]" for a Muslim homeland in the [[Deccan Plateau|Deccan]]. He also suggested ''Dinia'' as a name for a South Asia of various religions.{{sfnp|Jalal, Self and Sovereignty |2002|pp=392–393}}<ref name=Dinia>{{cite web |last=Ali |first=Choudhary Rahmat |title=India: The Continent of DINIA or The Country of DOOM? |url=http://www.shelleys.demon.co.uk/dinia.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306022222/http://www.shelleys.demon.co.uk/dinia.htm |archive-date=6 March 2012}}</ref>

== Conception of 'Pakistan' ==
[[File:Humberstone Road Cambridge.jpg|thumb|The house in Humberstone Road, Cambridge where Ali lived and wrote "Pakistan" for the first time.]]
Historian [[Aqeel Abbas Jafari]] has noted that that the name "Pakistan" was first used by a Kashmir Journalist, Ghulam Hassan Shah Kazmi on 1 July 1928,<ref>{{cite news
 |title=لفظ پاکستان کا خالق چوہدری رحمت علی یا کوئی اور؟ [Is the creator of the word Pakistan Chaudhry Rehmat Ali or someone else?]
 |url=https://www.dawnnews.tv/news/1075441/lafz-pakistan-ka-khaliq-chauhdry-rehmat-ali-ya-koi-aur-aqeel-abbas-jafri-bm-fp
 |work=[[Dawn (newspaper)]]
 |author=Aqeel Abbas Jafri
 |date=6 February 2019
 |access-date=16 December 2025
 |language=Urdu
}}</ref> when he moved an application before the government in [[Abbottabad]] seeking a sanction for publishing a weekly newspaper named "Pakistan". This is the first documented occasion that the word Pakistan had been used.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Handwara journalist gave Pakistan its name, research establishes |url=https://kashmirlife.net/a-handwara-journalist-gave-pakistan-its-name-research-establishes-169169/ |website=Kashmir Life |access-date=25 March 2018 |date=25 March 2018}}</ref> Choudhry Rahmat Ali is said to have suggested the name of the independent Muslim state Pakistan in 1933, 5 years after the name was adopted by Ghulam Hasan Shah Kazmi for his newspaper.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Name Pakistan Was Coined By A Kashmiri Journalist And Not Choudhry Rahmat Ali, Says New Research |url=https://www.outlookindia.com/website/story/the-name-pakistan-was-coined-by-a-kashmiri-journalist-and-not-choudhry-rahmat-al/310008 |website=www.outlookindia.com/ |date=26 March 2018 |access-date=26 March 2018}}</ref>

In 1930, Ali moved to a house in [[Cambridge]], on 3 Humberstone Road, it was in one of the rooms of this house that he is said to have written the word 'Pakistan' for the first time. According to Ali's secretary Miss Frost, he came up with the idea while riding on the top of a London bus.<ref>{{cite web |title=Meeting with Miss Frost, Rahmat Ali's former secretary |url=http://www.shelleys.demon.co.uk/Frost.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120316164159/http://www.shelleys.demon.co.uk/Frost.htm |archive-date=16 March 2012}}</ref>

After the creation of the name there are a couple of accounts of him first discussing it, according to a friend, Abdul Kareem Jabbar, the name came up when Ali was walking along the banks of the [[Thames]] in 1932 with his friends Pir Ahsan-ud-Din and Khwaja Abdul Rahim.  In the 1930s, the [[London General Omnibus Company]] (LGOC) operated numerous bus routes that served the banks of the River Thames, especially around central London (Westminster, Embankment, Blackfriars, Southwark, and Tower Bridge). Key services included Routes 11, 24, 59, and 76, which ran along or crossed near the Thames, linking north–south London and providing access to the Embankment and bridges.<ref name="LBUS">{{cite web
 |title=Pocket bus map No 11, 1930 issued by the London General Omnibus Company Ltd
 |url=https://www.ltmuseum.co.uk/collections/collections-online/maps/item/1992-335
 |website=London Transport Museum Collections Online
 |publisher=London Transport Museum
 |access-date=14 December 2025
 |language=English
}}</ref>

Sir [[Mohammad Iqbal]] said that Rahmat Ali visited him in [[London]] when he was there for the [[First Round Table Conference]] in 1930 and asked him what he would call the government of the Muslim state he had proposed in Allahabad. Iqbal told him that he would call it "Pakistan" as an acronym based on the provinces' names.<ref>{{harvp|Aziz|1987|p=352}}: "As the word Pakistan was then being attributed to Rahmat Ali, Waheed asked Iqbal about the truth of the matter and received this answer: "When I was in London in 1930 [sic.] for attending the Round Table Conference, Chaudhri Rahmat Ali came to see me once and asked me by what name the government [sic.] (''hakumat'') established under my Allahabad scheme would be called. On this, I told him that if you take the first word [Sic.] (''lafz'') of each province in the northwest of India and the 'tan' of Baluchistan, you get a meaningful and nice word, Pakistan. That will be the name of the government."</ref> In 1930, St. James’s Palace was served by several London General Omnibus Company (LGOC) routes running along Pall Mall, Piccadilly, and St. James’s Street, placing the palace within easy reach of central bus services. The most notable were Route 3, Route 12, and Route 38, which connected the West End to areas like Brixton, Dulwich, and Clapton.<ref name="LBUS"/>

According to Ali's biographer [[Khursheed Kamal Aziz]], the idea came to Ali in December 1932 "or a little earlier" while he was travelling on the top deck of a [[London Buses route 11|route 11 bus]], Aziz states that Ali had "told this to his secretary, Miss Frost, on returning to Cambridge" and that she in turn had told Aziz when he interviewed her. On the bus journey Ali had a eureka moment and the "word flashed on the screen of his mind."{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=89}}

On 28 January 1933, Ali voiced the idea in a pamphlet titled "[[s: Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?|Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?]]".<ref name="non">{{cite Wikisource |title=Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever? |author=Choudhary Rahmat Ali |year=1933}}</ref> The word 'Pakstan' referred to "the five Northern units of India, viz., [[Punjab (British India)|'''P'''unjab]], North-West Frontier Province ([[Afghania|'''A'''fghania]]), [[Kashmir region|'''K'''ashmir]], [[Sindh|'''S'''indh]] and [[Balochistan (Pakistan)|Baluchis'''tan''']]".<ref name="nowornever">{{citation|title=Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?|author1=Choudhary Rahmat Ali|author2=Mohd Aslam Khan |author3=Sheikh Mohd Sadiq |author4=Inayat Ullah Khan|date=28 January 1933}}: "At this solemn hour in the history of India, when British and Indian statesmen are laying the foundations of a Federal Constitution for that land, we address this appeal to you, in the name of our common heritage, on behalf of our thirty million Muslim brethren who live in PAKSTAN [sic] – by which we mean the five Northern units of India, viz., Punjab, North-West Frontier Province (Afghan Province), Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan – for your sympathy and support in our grim and fateful struggle against political crucifixion and complete annihilation."</ref><ref name="wolpert">
{{cite book |last=Wolpert |first=Stanley A. |author-link=Stanley Wolpert |title=Jinnah of Pakistan |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1984 |location=New York |isbn=0-19-503412-0}}
</ref> By the end of 1933, 'Pakistan' had become common vocabulary, and an '''i''' was added to ease pronunciation (as in Afghan-i-stan).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.storyofpakistan.com/person.asp?perid=P008|title=Chaudhry Rehmat Ali|work=Story of Pakistan|date=June 2003}}</ref> Ali also wrote that this would be followed by "reintegration of the three Muslim 'Asian' homelands of Afghanistan, Iran and Tajikistan" into Pakistan, a reference to Northwest India's political, historical and cultural affiliations with West Asia.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bianchini|first1=Stefano|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zsV_AgAAQBAJ&q=chaudhry+rehmat+ali+iran+afghanistan&pg=PT228|title=Partitions: Reshaping States and Minds|last2=Chaturvedi|first2=Sanjay|last3=Ivekovic|first3=Rada|last4=Samaddar|first4=Ranabir|date=2 August 2004|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-134-27653-0|language=en}}</ref>

In a subsequent book, Ali discussed the etymology in further detail:<ref name="Choudhry Rahmat Ali 1947">{{citation |last=RahmatʻAli |first=Choudhary |title=Pakistan: The Fatherland of the Pak Nation |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lPkJAQAAIAAJ |year=1978 |publisher=Book Traders |orig-year=first published 1947}}</ref> 'Pakistan' is both a Persian and an Urdu word. It is composed of letters taken from the names of all our South Asia homelands; that is, Punjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh and Balochistan. It means the land of the Paks – the spiritually pure and clean.

Ali's pamphlet described the Muslims of his proposed 'Pakistan' as a 'nation', which later formed the foundation for the [[two-nation theory]] of the [[All-India Muslim League]]:
{{Cquote|quote=Our religion and culture, our history and tradition, our social code and economic system, and our laws of inheritance, succession and marriage are fundamentally different from those of most people's living in the rest of India. The ideals which move our people to make the highest sacrifices are essentially different from those which inspire the Hindus to do the same. These differences are not confined to broad, basic principles. Far from it. They extend to the minutest details of our lives. We do not inter-dine; we do not inter-marry. Our national customs and calendars, even our diet and dress are different.|author=Choudhry Rahmat Ali in January 1933{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|pp=99–100}}}}
Ali believed that the delegates of the first and second Round Table Conferences committed 'an inexcusable blunder and an incredible betrayal' by accepting the principle of an All-India Federation. He demanded that the national status of the 30 million Muslims of the northwestern units be recognized, and a separate Federal Constitution be granted to them.{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|pp=99–100}}

Ali's biographer, [[K.K. Aziz|K. K. Aziz]] writes,{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=85}} "Rahmat Ali alone drafted this declaration"<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110419012150/http://www.chaudhryrahmatali.com/now%20or%20never/index.htm "Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?"]}}</ref> (in which the word Pakistan was used for the first time), but to make it "representative" he began to look around for people who would sign it along with him. This search did not prove easy, "for so firm was the grip of '[[Indian Nationalism|Muslim Indian Nationalism]]' on our young intellectuals at English universities that it took me (Rahmat Ali) more than a month to find three young men in London who offered to support and sign it." Later on, his political opponents used the name of these signatories and other friends of Ali, as creators of the word 'Pakistan'.

Choudhary Rehmat Ali was the personality who started independence movement in the name of Pakistan. He gave idea of two nations in 1915. He formed Pakistan National Movement in 1934 and also released fortnightly Pakistan newspaper in 1935.

== Opposition to "Indianism" ==
According to his writings, "[[Greater India|Indianism]]" meant emphasizing the abode and culture of the "caste [[Hindus]]" as the primary and essential constituent of a subcontinent-wide nation. It was in his view Indianism was "the designation of a State created by the [[British Raj|British]] for the first time in history", citing that the [[Indian National Congress]] being established in 1885 as evidence that Indianism originated in the hands of the British in the service of British imperialism. He criticizes the notion of the unity of "the country of India"; instead he considers it a continent with a wide variety of nations, ethnicities and religions, and that the [[Muslims]], [[Sikhs]], the [[Maratha (caste)|Marathas]], the [[Untouchables (caste)|Achhūts (untouchables)]] and the [[Rajput]]s were in fact separate nations, on whom the fetters of "Indianism" were fastened by imposing on all of them this "preposterous prefix of All-India".<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Bh4xDwAAQBAJ&dq=altaf+hussain+hali+emphasized&pg=PA90 |title=Muslims Against the Muslim League:Critiques of the Idea of Pakistan |date=2017 |page=93 |author= Ali Usman Qasmi |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781107166639 }}</ref>

==Iqbal and Jinnah==
[[File:Choudhry Rehmat Ali (seated first from left) with Muhammad Iqbal (center), Khawaja Abdul Rahim (right) and a group of other young activists during Iqbal visit to England in 1932..jpg#/media/File:Choudhry Rehmat Ali (seated first from left) with Muhammad Iqbal (center), Khawaja Abdul Rahim (right) and a group of other young activists during Iqbal visit to England in 1932..jpg|thumb|right|200px|
Choudhry Rahmat Ali (seated first from left) with Muhammad Iqbal (center), Khawaja Abdul Rahim (right) and a group of other young activists during Iqbal visit to England in 1932|link=File:Choudhry_Rehmat_Ali_(seated_first_from_left)_with_Muhammad_Iqbal_(center),_Khawaja_Abdul_Rahim_(right)_and_a_group_of_other_young_activists_during_Iqbal_visit_to_England_in_1932..jpg]]
On 29 December 1930, Muhammad Iqbal delivered his presidential address, wherein he said:<ref>A.R. Tariq (ed.), Speeches and Statements of Iqbal (Lahore: 1973),</ref>
{{blockquote|I would like to see Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Baluchistan amalgamated into a single State. Self-government within the British Empire, or without the British Empire, the formation of a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim State appears to me to be the final destiny of the Muslims, at least of North-West India.}}
According to some scholars,{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|pp=351–362}} Iqbal had not presented the idea of an autonomous Muslim State; rather he wanted a large Muslim province by amalgamating Punjab, Sindh, NWFP and Baluchistan into a big North-Western province within India.<ref>K. K. Aziz, ''Making of Pakistan'' (London: 1970), p. 81.</ref> They argue that Iqbal never called for any kind of partition of the country.<ref>Verinder Grover (ed.), Muhammad Iqbal: Poet Thinker of Modern Muslim India Vol. 25 (New Delhi: Deep & Deep Publications, 1995), pp. 666–67.</ref><ref>Tara Chand, History of Freedom Movement in India Vol. III (New Delhi: 1972), p. 253.</ref><ref>lang, 23, 24 & 25 March 2003;{{full citation needed|date=October 2018}} Also see, Safdar Mahmood, ''Iqbal, Jinnah aur Pakistan'' (Lahore: Khazina Ilm-was-Adab, 2004), pp. 52–69.</ref>

On 28 January 1933, Choudhry Rahmat Ali voiced his ideas on 'Pakistan'. By the end of 1933, the word "Pakistan" became common vocabulary where an "I" was added to ease pronunciation (as in Afghan-i-stan).
In a subsequent book Rahmat Ali discussed the etymology in further detail:
"'Pakistan' is both a Persian and an Urdu word. It is composed of letters taken from the names of all our homelands- " Indian " and " Asian." That is, '''P'''unjab, '''A'''fghania, '''K'''ashmir, '''I'''ran, '''S'''indh and Balochistan. It means the land of the Pure."<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rahmat Ali
 |first=Choudhary
 |title=Pakistan: The Fatherland of the Pak Nation
 |publisher=Pakistan National Movement
 |location=Cambridge
 |year=1947
 |url=https://archive.org/details/pakistanfatherla00rahm/page/224/mode/2up
 |access-date=13 December 2025
 |language=English
 |page=225
}}</ref>

[[Jawaharlal Nehru]] had written in his book on the scheme: "Iqbal was one of the early advocates of Pakistan and yet he appears to have realised its inherent danger and absurdity. Edward Thompson has written that in the course of the conversation, Iqbal told him that he had advocated Pakistan because of his position as President of the Muslim League session, but he felt sure that it would be injurious to India as a whole and Muslims especially."<ref>J.L. Nehru, Discovery of India (New York: 1946), p. 353.</ref>

In 1934, Choudhry Rahmat Ali and his friends met [[Muhammad Ali Jinnah]] and appealed for his support of the Pakistan idea. He replied, "My dear boys, don't be in a hurry; let the waters flow and they will find their own level."<ref name="Hiro2015">
{{citation|last=Hiro|first=Dilip|title=The Longest August: The Unflinching Rivalry Between India and Pakistan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t5g4DgAAQBAJ&pg=PT69|year=2015|publisher=PublicAffairs|isbn=978-1-56858-503-1|pages=69–}}
</ref><ref name="Bose2015">
{{citation|last=Bose|first=Madhuri|title=The Bose Brothers and Indian Independence: An Insider's Account|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MLSqCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA38-IA27|year=2015|publisher=SAGE Publications|isbn=978-93-5150-396-5|pages=38–}}
</ref>

==Proposed maps and names==
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:MAPOFRAHMATPLAN.jpg|thumb|right|200px|The Continent of Dinia proposed by Choudhry Rahmat Ali]] -->{{anchor|Dinia}}
Ali published several pamphlets where he called himself the "''Founder of the Pakistan National Movement''". In these pamphlets he included maps of the subcontinent with potential Muslim states, including Haideristan, Siddiqistan, Faruqistan, Muinistan and Maplistan.<ref name="Dawn_Karachi_2008" /> Safiistan and Nasaristan were proposed on [[Sri Lanka]].<ref name="FrankJacobs" />

In his maps he renamed the Indian subcontinent 'Pakasia' or more often 'Dinia' (an anagram of "India" with position of 'D' changed), meaning "Land of the Faith" in Arabic (from the word "deen"). Dinia was represented with dependencies Pakistan, Osmanistan (representing Hyderabad Deccan and neighbouring areas) and Bangistan (representing Bengal). He proposed the former Muslim provinces of [[Eastern Bengal and Assam]] in East India to become Bangistan, an independent Muslim state for Bengali, Assamese and Bihari Muslims. He proposed the princely [[Hyderabad State]], to become an Islamic monarchy called Osmanistan.{{sfnp|Jalal, Self and Sovereignty |2002|pp=392–393}}<ref name=Dinia/> Ali also renamed the seas around the Indian subcontinent, and referred the seas around landmass of Dinia as the Bangian, Pakian and Osmanian seas that were his proposed names for the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, and the Indian Ocean respectively.<ref name="Dawn_Karachi_2008" /><ref name="FrankJacobs">{{cite web |last1=Jacobs |first1=Frank |title=Purist Among the Pure: the Forgotten Inventor of Pakistan |url=https://bigthink.com/strange-maps/647-purist-among-the-pure-the-forgotten-inventor-of-pakistan |website=Big Think |access-date=28 January 2019 |language=en |date=5 March 2014}}</ref>

These alternate geographical maps of the subcontinent were followed by the mention of Rahmat Ali’s position as the "founder of the Siddiqistan, Nasaristan and Safiistan National Movements".<ref name="Dawn_Karachi_2008">{{cite news |title=KARACHI: Learning from history |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/316840 |access-date=28 January 2019 |publisher=DAWN.COM |date=17 August 2008 |language=en}}</ref> Ali even referred to the [[Andaman Islands|Andamans]] as the "Ashur Islands" and the [[Nicobar Islands|Nicobars]] as the "Balus Islands" in such maps.

Mian Abdul Haq, a contemporary of Rahmat Ali at the University of Cambridge, stated that, after 1935, Rahmat Ali's mental makeup changed resulting from a study of "major Nazi works, of which he knew many passages by heart."<ref>{{citation |last=Ikram |first=S.M. |title=Indian Muslims and Partition of India |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7q9EubOYZmwC&pg=PA177 |year=1995 |publisher=Atlantic Publishers & Dist |isbn=978-81-7156-374-6 |pages=177–178}}</ref>

== After the creation of Pakistan ==
While Choudhry Rahmat Ali was a leading figure for the conception of [[Dominion of Pakistan|Pakistan]], he lived most of his adult life in [[England]].

After the [[Partition of India|partition]] and creation of Pakistan in 1947, Ali returned to [[Lahore]], Pakistan on 6 April 1948. He had been voicing his dissatisfaction with the creation of Pakistan ever since his arrival in Lahore. He was unhappy over a smaller Pakistan than the one he had conceived in his 1933 pamphlet.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=469}} He condemned Jinnah for accepting a smaller Pakistan,{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|p=469}} calling him "Quisling-e-Azam."{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|p=82}}{{efn|The branding of Jinnah is found in Ali's 1947 pamphlet titled ''The Greatest Betrayal, the Millat’s Martyrdom & The Muslim’s Duty''. "Quisling" is an allusion to [[Vidkun Quisling]], a Norwegian leader who ran a puppet regime under [[Nazi]]s.{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|p=82}} Rahmat Ali may have introduced this term into South Asian politics, which was later used by the prime minister [[Liaquat Ali Khan]] to brand the Kashmiri leader [[Sheikh Abdullah]].<ref name="Gupta2012">{{citation |last=Das Gupta |first=Jyoti Bhusan |title=Jammu and Kashmir |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dpTpCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA72 |year=2012 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-94-011-9231-6 |pages=72–}}</ref>}}

Ali had planned to stay in the country, but he was expelled from Pakistan by the then Prime Minister [[Liaqat Ali Khan]]. His belongings were confiscated, and he left empty-handed for England in October 1948.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|pp=303, 316}}

==Death==
[[File:Grave of Choudhary Rahmat Ali.jpg|thumb|right|200px|[[Headstone]] of Ali's Grave]]
Ali died on 3 February 1951 in Cambridge. According to his secretary Thelma Frost, he was "destitute, forlorn and lonely" at the time of his death.{{sfnp|Kamran|2017|pp=87–88}} Fearing (correctly) that he may have died insolvent, the Master of [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]], [[Edward Welbourne]], instructed that the College would cover the funeral expenses. He was buried on 20 February at [[Cambridge City Cemetery]] in Cambridge, England.{{sfnp|Aziz|1987|pp=340–345}} The funeral expenses and other medical expenses were repaid by the High Commissioner for Pakistan in November 1953, after what was described as a “protracted correspondence” between the London office and the relevant authorities in Pakistan.<ref>Emmanuel College Cambridge Archives</ref>

His obituary in Emmanuel College Magazine 1950-51 (that covers the academic year starting in [[Michaelmas term]] 1950 and ending in [[Easter term]] 1951) notes: "It may not be the function of a College magazine to awaken the rancours of the politics of other lands, but it would be absurd not to record the fact that this obscure and single-handed undergraduate of Emmanuel College, who died in Cambridge in the [[Influenza pandemic|influenza epidemic]] of the spring of this year and who is buried in the Newmarket Road cemetery, has influenced world events, and may yet influence the future, more than falls to the lot of most men."<ref>{{cite news

== Legacy ==
Rahmat Ali is credited by Pakistanis for having coined the term "Pakistan" and envisioning a separate state for Muslims. Beyond that, his ideas are not explored in any detail.<ref>Karthik Venkatesh, [https://herald.dawn.com/news/1154042 All but forgotten: Choudhary Rahmat Ali, the inventor and first champion of Pakistan], Herald, 26 February 2018.</ref>

Ali's house in Cambridge has become a minor tourist attraction for Pakistani visitors. In an interview with the University of Cambridge's ''[[Varsity (Cambridge)|Varsity]]'' newspaper, the current owner of the house, Juliet Mills, said they "do get people coming to the door asking to look around".<ref>{{cite news

extract:
Choudhry Rahmat Ali (16 November 1897 – 3 February 1951) was a Muslim nationalist activist who is credited with coining the name "Pakistan" for a separate Muslim homeland in British India and is sometimes regarded as the originator of the Pakistan Movement.
Born in Balachaur, Punjab, Rahmat Ali got his education in Lahore. His seminal contribution was when he was a law student at the University of Cambridge in 1933, in the form of a pamphlet "Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish Forever?", also known as the "Pakistan Declaration". The pamphlet was addressed to the British and Indian delegates to the Third Round Table Conference in London. The ideas did not find favour with the delegates or any of the politicians for close to a decade. They were dismissed as students' ideas particularly by Muhammad Ali Jinnah but, by 1940, the Muslim politicians in the subcontinent came around to accept them, leading to the Lahore Resolution of the All-India Muslim League, which was immediately dubbed the "Pakistan Resolution" in the press.
After the creation of Pakistan, Ali returned from England in April 1948, planning to stay in the country, but his belongings were confiscated and he was expelled by Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan. In October 1948, Ali left empty-handed. He died on 3 February 1951 in Cambridge "destitute, forlorn and lonely". The funeral expenses of insolvent Ali were covered by Emmanuel College, Cambridge on the instructions of its Master - Edward Welbourne. Ali was buried on 20 February 1951 at Cambridge City Cemetery.
